title: Photosynthesis
blurb: How plants eat sunlight and air.

items.front: Where does the mass of a tree actually come from?
items.back: Mostly carbon pulled out of the air, not nutrients from the soil.

items.front: What are the two inputs to photosynthesis?
items.back: Carbon dioxide and water, powered by light.
Chlorophyll, which absorbs red and blue and reflects green.

items.front: What is the waste product of photosynthesis?
items.back: Oxygen. Every breath you take is plant exhaust.

items.front: Where in the cell does it happen?
items.back: In chloroplasts, which have their own DNA from an ancient bacterium.
items.hook: A stowaway with its own DNA.

items.back: Glucose, which the plant burns for energy or stores as starch.

items.text: A mature oak pulls roughly 22 kg of carbon dioxide out of the air every year, and most of that becomes the tree itself.
Photosynthesis converts less than 1% of the sunlight that hits a leaf into stored energy, which is worse than a cheap solar panel.
Chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria that got swallowed and never left, which is why they still carry their own DNA.

quiz.q: Most of a tree's mass comes from:
quiz.explain: Carbon dioxide is pulled from the air and built into the wood itself.

quiz.q: Which pair are the raw inputs?
quiz.explain: Light supplies the energy; CO2 and water supply the atoms.
It absorbs red and blue and bounces green back at your eyes.

quiz.q: Oxygen in the atmosphere is best described as:
quiz.explain: The plant wants the sugar. Oxygen is what it throws away.

quiz.q: Chloroplasts have their own DNA because they:
quiz.explain: Endosymbiosis: one cell swallowed another and they never separated.
Glucose gets burned for energy or chained up into starch for storage.

quiz.q: Roughly how much CO2 does a mature oak absorb per year?
quiz.explain: Around 22 kg, and most of it ends up as the tree's own body.

quiz.q: Photosynthesis captures what share of the sunlight hitting a leaf?
quiz.explain: Under 1%. A cheap solar panel beats a leaf handily.

quiz.q: Chloroplasts carry their own DNA because they:
quiz.explain: They are the descendants of a bacterium that moved in permanently.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Okay. A tree weighs two tons. Where did the two tons come from?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: The soil, obviously. It grew out of the ground.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That is what everyone says, and it is wrong. Dig up a tree and the hole is basically the same size.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Wait. So where is the tree coming from?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The air. It is pulling carbon dioxide out of the sky and building itself out of it. A tree is mostly air that stopped moving.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That is genuinely unsettling and I love it.

quiz_after.q: So a tree's mass mostly comes from...
quiz_after.reaction_correct: Exactly. You are standing in a forest made of sky.
quiz_after.reaction_wrong: Nope, the air. Honestly I got that wrong too the first time.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Here is the part nobody tells you. Chlorophyll is bad at its job.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Bad how? It runs the entire planet.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It throws away green light. Green is the brightest part of sunlight and the leaf just bounces it back.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So leaves are green because that is the light they refuse to use?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Correct. The colour of every plant on Earth is a rejection notice.

quiz_after.reaction_correct: Right. You are looking at the light plants did not want.
quiz_after.reaction_wrong: Other way round. It reflects green, which is why you see it.

coach_system: You are a warm, sharp tutor quizzing someone on photosynthesis. Ask ONE short question at a time and react to their answer honestly - correct them when they are wrong. Keep every reply under 40 words and sound like a person, not a textbook.
